items.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
items.summary: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are now available on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Learn what's new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with it on Amazon Bedrock.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS

 Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences.

 In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock.

 Why Claude Fable 5.2

 Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes.

 In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly.

 If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit.

 For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs .

 Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 use cases

 Where Fable 5.2 fits:

 Agentic coding across large, multi-repository codebases.

 Long-running agents for coordinating many subagents on multi-day work.

 Scientific research from new analytical methods to formal mathematical proofs.

 Financial analysis for quantitative research and forecasting.

 Design for 3D, hardware, and motion for generating environments, components, and simulations in code.

 Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier:

 Cyber security , for security engineering, red teaming, and penetration testing.

 Life sciences research , especially biomolecular design and research synthesis.

 Data retention and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

 Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details.

 Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS works by storing data in cloud infrastructure controlled by the customer. Until EFS is available, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention. This is available for internal use through at least June 30, 2027.

 Getting started with Claude Fable 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock

 To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it.

 Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime (through the Anthropic SDK). You can also stay on the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK .

 Prerequisites

 To follow along with the code examples in this post, you need the following:

 An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access.

 AWS CLI installed and configured with appropriate credentials.

 Python 3.9 or later.

 Boto3 (AWS SDK for Python) installed: pip install boto3 .

 AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions: bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream .

 Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3):

 import boto3
import json

# Create a Bedrock Runtime client
bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(
 service_name="bedrock-runtime",
 region_name="us-east-1"
)

# Invoke Claude Fable 5.2
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
 modelId="global.anthropic.claude-fable-5-2",
 contentType="application/json",
 accept="application/json",
 body=json.dumps({
 "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31",
 "max_tokens": 4096,
 "messages": [
 {
 "role": "user",
 "content": "An S3 bucket serves 40 TB/month egress. Estimate the monthly egress cost at $0.09/GB, and state one architecture change, using AWS services, to cut it. Show the calculation, keep it under 120 words."
 }
 ]
 })
)

result = json.loads(response["body"].read())

# Fable 5.2 is a reasoning model: the response may include a thinking block
# before the text block, so select the text block rather than a fixed index.
print(next(b["text"] for b in result["content"] if b["type"] == "text")) 

 You can explore the Getting Started notebook for more examples.

 Migrating to Claude Fable 5.2 with the claude-api skill in Claude Code

 For teams already running Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, the claude-api skill in Claude Code helps you upgrade to Fable 5.2.

 The claude-api skill is an open-source skill built into Claude Code that captures the details that make Claude API code work well. It covers which agent patterns fit a given job, what parameters change between model generations, and when to apply prompt caching. It stays current as Anthropic’s SDKs evolve: when a new model is released or the API gains a feature, the skill already knows.

 What the skill does for Fable 5.2 migrations

 When you ask Claude Code to upgrade your codebase to Fable 5.2, the skill reviews your code and walks you through:

 Updating model references swapping model IDs to the Fable 5.2 ID across your application code.

 Adjusting thinking settings moving manual thinking configurations to adaptive thinking where appropriate for the new model.

 Cleaning up outdated parameters removing deprecated beta headers, parameters, and settings that no longer apply.

 Suggesting effort levels recommending the right output_config.effort settings inline based on your use case.

 The skill also detects your deployment platform including Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, and other environments and adjusts model ID formats and feature configurations accordingly. For example, it uses the Amazon Bedrock structured model ID format ( global.anthropic.claude-fable-5-2 ).

 How to use it

 In Claude Code, run the migration directly:

 /claude-api migrate 

 This scans your working directory (or a subdirectory or specific file list you confirm) and applies the migration changes in a single guided pass. You can also invoke it conversationally by telling Claude Code:

 “Upgrade me to Claude Fable 5.2” Claude reviews your code and walks through the necessary changes.

 “Improve my cache hit rate” the skill applies prompt caching rules that many developers miss, helping reduce costs on Bedrock.

 “Add context compaction to my agent” it walks you through compaction primitives and agent patterns for long-running Fable 5.2 sessions.

 The claude-api skill is available in Claude Code and is also bundled into CodeRabbit, JetBrains IDEs (including Junie), Resolve AI, and Warp. It is open source at anthropics/skills on GitHub, so any coding agent can integrate it.

 Availability

 Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are available today on Amazon Bedrock through US Geo CRIS and Global CRIS inference profiles. See the Bedrock documentation for the full list of supported Regions. For pricing information, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Both models are also available through Claude Platform on AWS in every Region where the service is offered.

 Give Claude Fable 5.2 a try in the Amazon Bedrock console , in Claude Platform on AWS , or explore the Getting Started notebook on GitHub.

 About the authors

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
items.summary: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B-parameter multimodal vision-language model, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Deploy the NVFP4 or BF16 variant in a few steps, then run text, image, and video inference for document intelligence, computer-use agents, and multimodal agentic workloads.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart

 Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text.

 The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request.

 NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference.

 Model overview

 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder.

 Language backbone : 88 layers that interleave Mamba-2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) with 8 attention layers, plus a shared MTP head. The backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base.

 Vision encoder : A C-RADIO vision encoder encodes images and sampled video frames, and a vision-language connector maps them into the language backbone’s embedding space. The encoder and connector stay in BF16 in both variants.

 Training : The model first goes through continued pre-training, long-context and software-engineering mid-training, and vision-language training. It then goes through two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long-context data. Next come reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and human feedback in NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and a final stage that further trains the MTP head. The NVFP4 checkpoint is produced from BF16 with NVIDIA Model Optimizer and quantization-aware distillation. It keeps the vision encoder, connector, Mamba convolutions, and embeddings in BF16 and the MoE router in FP32. It runs with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) on Blackwell GPUs.

 Key use cases

 Super VL is aimed at agentic workloads that must see and read. It targets vision-language agents that combine reasoning, coding, tool use, document understanding, and video understanding.

 Document intelligence : Optical character recognition (OCR), charts, tables, and multipage documents. Each 1,536 x 1,024 page image costs about 1,536 tokens of context. The JumpStart serving configuration accepts one image and one video per request.

 GUI understanding : Screen grounding and reasoning for computer-use agents that navigate applications.

 Video understanding : Analyze and summarize short MP4 video clips, including answering questions about visual content. You can provide videos inline as base64-encoded content, subject to the endpoint’s request payload size limits.

 Multimodal agents : Tool calling, JSON schema output through response_format , and configurable reasoning support multimodal agent workflows.

 Customization (BF16) : Download the BF16 reference weights for SFT, RL, distillation, domain adaptation, or creating your own quantized variants. The JumpStart endpoint serves the base weights only and does not load LoRA adapters.

 Model-quality benchmarks

 The NVIDIA model cards report results for both checkpoints across reasoning, coding, agentic, long-context, and multimodal benchmarks, with evaluation settings held constant so that only the checkpoint differs. For the full comparison against other publicly available models and the evaluation settings, see the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning Technical Report .

 Inference performance on SageMaker JumpStart

 We measured inference performance with the JumpStart release container using the generate workload profile: 250 input tokens, 1,500 output tokens, and five concurrent streaming requests. Throughput is the mean output tokens per second for each request, and time to first token is the mean across requests.

The BF16 variant on ml.p5en.48xlarge achieved 140.85 output tokens per second per request in this test. Time to first token remained about half a second across all three configurations. Because the variants run on different GPU systems and configurations, these measurements are not an isolated BF16-versus-NVFP4 precision comparison. Longer prompts change the picture: with the summarize profile (10,000 input tokens), time to first token on ml.g7.24xlarge is 12.62 seconds.

 Supported instances

 SageMaker JumpStart supports Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the following validated instance types. NVFP4 runs on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and BF16 runs on P5en instances with NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The JumpStart default instance for NVFP4 is ml.g7.24xlarge, which serves as the recommended starting point for the generate profile.

 You can deploy the model from SageMaker Studio, with the SageMaker Python SDK, or from the Hugging Face model page.

 Prerequisites

 Before you deploy, make sure you have the following:

 An AWS account with permissions to create Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints.

 An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with access to SageMaker AI.

 Service quota for ml.g7.24xlarge, ml.g7.48xlarge, or ml.p5en.48xlarge endpoint usage. The ml.g7 quotas start at zero in new accounts, so request an increase through Service Quotas before you deploy.

items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Professional work deserves professional tools. Meet AWS Quick.

 Our first brand campaign celebrates teams who keep business moving and the AI workspace built only for them. Every day, teams at leading enterprises use AWS Quick to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Today we’re launching our first brand campaign to bring that same experience to millions more knowledge workers around the world. The campaign runs across the United States and the United Kingdom on streaming TV, online video, social media, and leading business publications. AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work, where teams use AI agents to research, analyze, and act across the data and applications they already rely on. Across virtually every industry, leading enterprises including 3M, BMW, Mondelez, New York Life, and Southwest Airlines are using Quick to transform how they work. The campaign celebrates the teams who know that the work they do every day deserves tools built for it.

 The work you know

 Customers tell us their AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains stay personal. A sales rep still builds territory plans by pulling from the CRM, dashboards, call notes, and email. Because context stays locked inside a single project or one vendor’s suite, productivity never compounds across the team or the company. Most of those tools started as consumer apps and still serve personal and professional use with the same product. AWS Quick took the opposite path: it was built for work from day one, on the same AWS infrastructure that millions of customers use to run their mission-critical applications. These include many of the world’s most complex and security-sensitive workloads.

 Built for your business from day one

 AWS Quick has no consumer version. Every roadmap decision and every feature we ship starts with one question: does it help individuals, teams, and entire enterprises do their most important work? Quick knows your role, your team, and how your projects, people, and data connect, because it works across the applications and workflows your teams already use. Quick watches for changes, surfaces what matters, and acts on your behalf, which leaves your team free to focus on what moves the business forward. Anyone can build agents, apps, and automations by describing what they need in plain language, without filing an IT ticket. Everything built in a shared space becomes an asset the whole team can use.

 Trust built in

 Quick is integrated with the security and compliance tools you already use, including Microsoft Purview for data protection, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and Microsoft Active Directory for permission-based controls. Quick reads the sensitivity labels already on your files, enforces existing permissions, and flags potentially sensitive data to administrators. Assets including agents, knowledge bases, and skills reach new teams only through approved sharing, and every approval and denial is recorded with who decided, what they shared, and why. Quick also carries the compliance certifications most organizations require, including HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, and ISO 27001. Your data is yours, and your conversations are private. No one else can browse your conversations, and IT admins cannot access your chat transcripts. Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail are built in, giving your organization a full audit trail of what happened, who did it, and when. Your data never leaves your environment and never trains someone else’s models.

 That commitment is also why we’re now AWS Quick, a name that signals the enterprise security and governance that have been part of Quick from the start.

 Every decision stays yours

 IT leaders, account executives, program managers, and finance leads all work differently, and Quick works the way each of them does, on any device and on their schedule. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.

 Ready to transform how your users, teams, and entire enterprise do their best work with an AI built for business? You can download Quick today and get started in minutes , or talk to your AWS account team about options for enterprise pricing plans.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.
items.content:
Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

 - Google Developers Blog

 Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

 NOV. 9, 2026

 Michael Tran 

 Software Engineering Intern 

 Google Cloud 

 Nuojin Cheng 

 Software Engineer 

 Google Cloud 

 Deepak Patil 

 Group Product Manager 

 Share 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 LinkedIn 

 Mail 

 Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.
 In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:

 Attention Compute: At long context, attention FLOPs grow quadratically with sequence length and attention dominates the training step. Throughput depends on the attention kernel.
 Memory and Communication: Activations, including the aggregate volume of keys and values for every token, grow with sequence length. Replicating them on every chip, as a naive all-gather does, exhausts high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and triggers out-of-memory failures. In addition, memory-related constraints force communication and recomputation which could negatively impact Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU). The fix here is context parallelism (CP) that streams keys and values instead of materializing them in full.

 Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText , Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU : All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention) , and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP) , combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel . Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.
 This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4 ( doc ).
 Context Parallelism in MaxText
 Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.
 Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).
 All-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

 Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

 Figure 1. All-gather, for one sequence split across four devices (TPU chips). Every device collects all keys and values, then attends locally. Outlined blocks mark attention being computed; small outlined blocks are data in flight.

 All-to-All (Ulysses): Gathering keys and values makes every chip hold the whole sequence, so attention memory never shrinks no matter how many chips you add. All-to-All changes what each chip owns instead. Attention is independent across heads but not across tokens, so the head axis is free to shard and the token axis is not. An All-to-All before attention rotates the sharding from one onto the other: each chip gives up the heads it is not responsible for and receives the tokens it was missing for the heads it keeps, ending up with the full sequence for a few heads instead of a few tokens for all heads. This is also why Ulysses does not need token load balancing. Attention then runs as ordinary single-chip attention with standard kernels, and a second All-to-All rotates the output back. KV per chip shrinks by the context-parallel factor, but you cannot split across more chips than the model has heads — and tensor parallelism shards that same dimension, so TP × CP is capped by the head count (under GQA, by the KV heads: eight for Llama 3 8B). The all-to-all itself, though, does not overlap with compute — attention cannot start on a partial sequence, so every chip waits for data from every other chip before any of them begins.

 Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

 Figure 2. All-to-All (Ulysses). An all-to-all trades token chunks for attention heads (the rows). Each device attends over the full sequence for its head, and the outputs return with a second all-to-all.

 P2P (ring attention): Ulysses' ceiling is the head count; ring attention removes it by never leaving the token axis. Keys and values never materialize in full. KV chunks travel around a ring of chips one hop at a time, neighbor to neighbor. Each chip attends its queries to the chunk it holds while the next one is in flight, and merges the partial results as it goes. A chip holds its own chunk and one visiting chunk, never the full sequence, and the communication overlaps compute. However, dividing attention computation into smaller chunks can reduce local kernel efficiency, and unlike All-to-All Ulysses, ring attention requires explicit load balancing.

 Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

 Figure 3. P2P (ring attention). KV chunks rotate one hop at a time. Each device attends to the chunk it holds while the next one arrives, and holds only one visiting chunk at a time.

 A2A + P2P (USP): A2A + P2P (USP): Neither strategy scales on its own — All-to-All stops at the head count, and a long ring accumulates hops while thinning the overlap that makes it work. Unified sequence parallelism composes them on two axes of the chip mesh, so the context-parallel degree becomes the product of the two: All-to-All along one axis, sized at or below the KV-head count, and a ring along the other to extend past it. Because each All-to-All group has already pooled its tokens, a ring step now carries a chunk larger by the All-to-All factor, and the ring is correspondingly shorter — more compute per hop to hide the transfer behind, and fewer hops to accumulate latency and causal imbalance. On Cloud TPU the two map onto two axes of the slice's chip mesh.

 Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

 Figure 4. A2A + P2P (USP). The all-to-all runs within each pair of devices and the P2P ring across the pairs, so each device attends over longer chunks with fewer hops.

 These strategies cover the attention variants in today's major models, from multi-head and grouped-query attention to DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.
 Built on a fast attention kernel 
 Splitting the sequence only pays off if the attention compute on each chip stays efficient. All four strategies run on Splash Attention, the block-sparse flash attention kernel from Tokamax , Google's open-source library of TPU kernels. It skips fully masked blocks and handles packed sequences without padding. P2P calls it once per ring step, on the local queries and the KV chunk that has just arrived, while the transfer for the next step runs underneath, in the forward and backward pass alike. Each chip does the same fused, block-level work it would do without context parallelism, with the communication hidden behind it.
 Context Parallelism Strategies and TPU Performance 
 P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice. We compare how far each can push context length on a fixed 64-chip TPU 5p slice with Llama 3.1 8B (256 head dim, 16 query heads) , and measure their MFUs. In ideal settings where both strategies can have large enough chunks (S/CP) and local batch size - the two major variables driving MFU on TPU 5p, we observe that P2P can outperform All-Gather almost every context length from 64K to 14M tokens, where communication becomes mostly hidden with the Ring circular transport schedule.

items.title: Introducing GIFT-Eval-CTX: An Open-Source Benchmark for Contextual Forecasting
items.summary: Built by Salesforce AI Research, GIFT-Eval-CTX measures how effectively LLMs and agentic AI convert forward-looking context, such as promotions or weather events, into precise forecasts. The benchmark demonstrates that feeding structured operational context…
items.content:
Share article

 Built by Salesforce AI Research, GIFT-Eval-CTX measures how effectively LLMs and agentic AI convert forward-looking context, such as promotions or weather events, into precise forecasts. The benchmark demonstrates that feeding structured operational context into agentic AI drastically cuts error rates, turning static predictions into reliable, proactive planning.

 Moving Beyond Historical Data 

 In enterprise operations, traditional time-series forecasting relies on a single premise: the past predicts the future. 

 Whether you are managing energy grid loads, optimizing logistics for global supply chains, scaling cloud infrastructure, or balancing retail inventory, traditional time series foundation models (TSFMs) analyze historical trends, seasonality, and variance to project what comes next.

 However, the real world rarely operates on autopilot. 

 An energy operator knows a heatwave is coming, a supply chain director knows a road closure will divert freight, and an IT leader knows a software release will spike server load. In these moments, historical data falls short because the critical insights live in a forward-looking business context.  

 TSFMs, such as Moirai-2 , learn from large collections of time series and can forecast new ones without additional training. But their standard interfaces primarily accept numerical history and predefined variables. Incorporating open-ended information from documents, plans, or expert judgment presents a different challenge.

 Contextual forecasting brings that information into the prediction process. It requires understanding what the context implies about the future and translating those implications into numerical forecasts. Large language models (LLMs) offer a way to interpret diverse contextual information. But their ability to transform this knowledge into numerical predictions remains unclear.

 To develop and compare LLM-based approaches, we need a consistent way to measure their abilities. GIFT-Eval-CTX asks:

 Given reliable information about future changes, can forecasting systems turn it into accurate numerical forecasts? 

 Inside GIFT-Eval-CTX 

 Expanding on Salesforce’s flagship GIFT-Eval benchmark , GIFT-Eval-CTX evaluates models across 10,000 tasks from 20 real-world datasets spanning energy, logistics, weather, retail, and cloud operations.

 Instead of relying on inconsistent free-form text, an automated pipeline extracts future operational data into standardized structured effects to measure how accurately forecasting systems turn context into numerical forecasts.

 Structured Effects: Macro Trends & Micro Disruptions 

 GIFT-Eval-CTX categorizes future context into two actionable layers:

 Macro Effects (The Big Picture): Tracks horizon-wide behavior, including overall trends (rising, falling, flat), seasonal cycles, and value bounds.

 Micro Effects (Localized Events): Pinpoints specific time windows and scales for three event types:

 Excursions: Temporary spikes or drops (e.g., Black Friday traffic or server outages).

 Mean Shifts: Permanent baseline level changes (e.g., opening a new facility).

 Seasonal Changes: Shifts in recurring cycles (e.g., altered store hours).

 Together, these layers give the AI the future’s shape and key events, leaving the model to fill in the exact step by step numbers.

 Figure 1: Overview of the GIFT-Eval-CTX framework. Forward-looking operational context is decomposed into horizon wide Macro trends and localized Micro effects to guide forecasting systems. 

 How the Benchmark Is Constructed 

 GIFT-Eval-CTX specifically selects difficult test windows where traditional time-series models fail using past data alone. Following rigorous automated critique and human spot-checking, the final benchmark encompasses 23,476 validated Micro effects paired with corresponding Macro horizon annotations. The data annotation pipeline includes:

 Discovery Agents: Scan trends and actual outcomes to map Macro patterns and locate where traditional models missed local events.

 Code Validation: Agents run deterministic code tools to test annotations against raw data and fix mathematical errors.

 Joint Critic Agent: An independent reviewer inspects the raw data to validate, reject, or refine annotations before final inclusion.

 Key Benchmark Takeaways 

 Forward-Looking Context Significantly Cuts Error 
 While pure LLMs underperform traditional forecasting models when given history alone, adding structured future context reduces forecasting error dramatically: GPT-5.6 Sol’s error dropped by 40.7% and Claude Opus 4.8’s by 29.6% .

 Agentic Systems Deliver The Best Accuracy 
 Combining an LLM with domain-specific models and code execution (MoiraiAgent) delivered the top performance across every forecast length. MoiraiAgent achieved an aggregate error score 36.3% lower than the best history only forecasting model , with its advantage widening on longer forecasts.

 Micro Effects Improve Overall Forecast Structure 
 Beyond localized accuracy, providing event context helps agents navigate transitions between multiple events and preserve critical repeating cycles (e.g., daily electricity demand patterns) that standard models flatten over time.

 Table 1: Comparative evaluation across forecasting systems measured by aggregated MASE scores (lower is better). Incorporating structured future context yields significant error reductions across frontier LLMs, with tool-augmented agentic architectures (MoiraiAgent) achieving superior accuracy across all forecast horizons. 

 Relying on Pure LLMs for Forecasting Is a Risk 

 Testing revealed a major flaw in relying on pure LLMs for raw forecasting: they struggle with numerical precision and output length. 

 Without tools, GPT-5.6 Sol generated the correct forecast length in only 38.9%–40.5% of medium-to-long tasks, while Claude Opus 4.8 succeeded in less than 2.3% .

 MoiraiAgent solves this through a two-step tool architecture: 

 Foundation Service Call: Calls the Moirai-2 engine to establish a mathematically complete numerical baseline of the exact required length.

 Code Execution: Uses code tools to calculate exact mathematical targets, apply context adjustments, and verify constraint compliance before outputting final results.

 The Future of Forecasting is here  

 The findings from GIFT-Eval-CTX highlight a critical milestone in AI-driven enterprise planning: feed AI systems structured future context, and forecasting accuracy leaps dramatically. To help researchers, developers, and enterprise teams evaluate and build the next wave of context aware forecasting systems, Salesforce AI Research has made the GIFT-Eval-CTX benchmark, dataset, and leaderboard fully open source. Explore our resources below and join us in advancing the future of intelligent operational planning.

items.title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
items.summary: Repeatable tasks like status updates, release notes, and ticket creation can be encoded in AWS Quick through agents and skills. This post covers how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, how to build and share skills for your team, and how the official catalog and custom agents help you use them.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 How skills and agents work in AWS Quick

 If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications.

 In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use.

 Understanding foundational concepts

 In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data.

 Figure 1: How a Quick agent follows its instructions, loads the skills a task needs, acts through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data

 The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards.

 Working with agents

 An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine . Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do.

 Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick.

 A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After you test and publish it, you can share it with other users and groups within your AWS Quick account. For a walkthrough of building one, see Build AI-powered employee onboarding agents with AWS Quick .

 Working with data

 Agents ground their answers in the data you connect to Quick. A space is a curated collection of documents and AWS Quick resources that an agent uses as a source of information. You can create one for yourself, your team, or another group in your organization. You can upload files and folders to a space, or add assets such as dashboards, knowledge bases, action connectors, and datasets. When you start a conversation with Quick, you can attach a space to narrow the data that Quick uses for that conversation. When you add a space to an agent, the space becomes part of the agent’s configuration, and the agent draws on it when a request needs it.

 A knowledge base is an organized, indexed collection of documents or content from data sources, optimized for retrieval and question answering. Quick syncs knowledge bases from sources such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), web crawler, or Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases . Quick keeps them up to date on a sync schedule.

 Datasets and dashboards come from AWS Quick Sight , the business intelligence feature in Quick, which is available in accounts provisioned through the AWS Management Console. A dataset is a prepared collection of data ready for use in analyses and dashboards. A dashboard is the published version of an analysis that you share with other Quick users. With datasets, you can build semantically rich metadata over your structured data, such as database tables, so you can accomplish complex analytical use cases with natural language.

 Lastly, a connector links AWS Quick to an external application or a native tool, so agents can read data and take action on your behalf. Cloud connectors connect Quick to services such as Microsoft Outlook, Slack, Jira, Asana, and Salesforce, and to remotely hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. They’re available on every device where you use Quick. Local connectors run on your own machine, such as an MCP server that you host yourself, so their tools are available only when that machine is on and connected. For the full list of connector types, see Connectors and Integration-specific guides in the AWS Quick User Guide.

 Together, these make your data, documents, and applications available through natural language, so you can ask questions and take actions in your connected sources.

 Working with skills

 A skill is a reusable set of instructions that teaches an agent how to do a specific task. Skills are also the foundation of how an agent in Quick behaves and completes work. Like other agents, an agent in Quick runs in a harness (a managed agent loop) that follows the reasoning and acting (ReAct) pattern. When you supply AWS Quick with a prompt, the agent uses its available tools and instructions to accomplish its goal and supply you with a response. Agent frameworks such as the Strands Agents SDK are built around the same model-driven loop.

 Much of what Quick does by default comes from system skills . For example, you can ask Quick to generate a Word document, a PowerPoint presentation, an Excel spreadsheet, or a PDF. A system skill can then create or edit the document using code with scripts the skill bundles. Other system skills browse the web, run code, execute deep research, transcribe audio and video, and generate images. Some manage Quick itself, such as building AWS Quick Flows , scheduling routines, handing work to a coding agent such as Kiro, managing your memories and knowledge graph, or tracking your to-dos. Within Quick, you can turn system skills on or off, but you can’t edit, duplicate, export, publish, share, or delete them.

 Skills can do many kinds of work because of the capabilities and tools that AWS Quick supplies. For example, one skill can produce a deliverable, such as a weekly status update built from your template. Another can automate a workflow across your connectors, such as gathering the week’s Jira updates and posting a summary to Slack. A skill can also run calculations in Python scripts and chart the results with JavaScript.

 What is a skill?

 Quick skills follow the Agent Skills specification, which Anthropic originally developed and released as an open standard. AWS Quick on desktop, which launched in preview in April 2026 and became generally available in September 2026 , uses this specification.

 A skill is a folder with a Markdown file SKILL.md at its root, plus any optional scripts or other reference files its instructions use. The file’s frontmatter, the attributes between two --- lines, holds the name, description, and any other metadata relevant to your skill. See the following shortened example of a skill named release-notes-generator .

 ---
name: release-notes-generator
description: "Generates human-readable release notes from merged pull requests, commits, or changelogs ... Use when asked to 'generate release notes', 'write changelog', ..."
--- 

 The description and name are the two most important aspects to triggering a skill. Quick uses progressive disclosure when it loads your skills into the agent’s prompt. The agent reads only each skill’s name and description until a request calls for that skill. It then loads the skill’s full instructions, as How agents load skills describes. This means certain phrases can help trigger the skill, such as “generate my release notes for version 2.3.” The specification caps name at 64 characters and description at 1,024, and recommends instructions within the skill to be under 5,000 tokens.

 Figure 2: The release-notes-generator skill folder, with a required SKILL.md file plus optional scripts and references folders

 Build and share a skill in Quick

 You can create a skill from chat, from a file (a .md or .zip file), or from a folder that has a SKILL.md file at its root. This post focuses on chat. To start, describe your task to Quick in chat. For example, you can start with this template (replace the content between <> brackets with your requirements):

 Every <specify your cadence e.g. every day, on monday, or none at all>, I have to grab data from the following sources:
- <List your sources and how you want to query them>
...

And do <describe how you want to transform the data and the exact sequence of steps>. 

Once I am finished, I have to create a report <describe your report format or provide an example> and send to the following stakeholders <describe your recipients> using the following connector <describe your connector>.

Create a skill from this requirement, and help me come up with testing scenarios to test the skill. 

 This is all you need to start building your own skills. Alternatively, you also can take a multi-turn conversation that you previously interacted with to accomplish a task and ask Quick to generate a skill from it. After you are satisfied with the final result, publish and share your skill:

 Choose Customize , and then choose Skills .

 Find your skill in draft, and open its detail panel.

 Choose Publish .

 Choose Share , and then choose the people or groups to share it with.

 Publishing and sharing are separate steps, so publishing alone doesn’t give anyone access to the skill. The people you share it with add it from Add to Quick under Shared wit

items.title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
items.summary: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot RAG and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream, alongside agentic retrieval. This post explains how the maxAgentIteration parameter matches retrieval effort to each request, using an illustrative internal banking policy assistant.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

 A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions.

 Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison.

 In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer.

 Key benefits

 Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit.

 For application builders, this provides several benefits:

 Better support for multi-part questions –  Targeted searches can find evidence for each part of a question instead of relying on one search to cover everything. In the banking example, the assistant can look up requirements for sole proprietors and LLCs separately before comparing them.

 Follow-up searches when information is missing – The planner can use what it finds to decide what to search for next. It can also retrieve a full document when a passage doesn’t provide enough context, helping address gaps that a single retrieval might leave unresolved.

 Answers with supporting evidence –  When response generation is enabled, the service combines retrieved information into an answer with citations. Trace events show the planning and retrieval steps, helping developers inspect how the answer was produced.

 Less custom orchestration – The service manages the planning, retrieval, evaluation, and response-generation workflow through one API. Applications don’t need to implement their own loop to coordinate these steps.

 These agentic capabilities remain valuable for complex questions. For straightforward lookups, applications also need a way to retrieve and answer without additional planning. The expanded maxAgentIteration range closes that gap. With one parameter, you can choose one of three modes for each request:

 Retrieval-only returns passages without generating an answer.

 Single-shot RAG retrieves once and generates an answer, with no planning rounds.

 Agentic retrieval plans and runs multiple searches for complex questions.

 Single-shot RAG uses one foundation model call to generate the answer, which can reduce latency and model usage compared with agentic retrieval. Retrieval-only requests make no foundation model calls. You can balance speed and answer quality for each request, without integrating a second API or maintaining separate code paths for simple and complex queries.

 How retrieval iterations are counted

 Before walking through the new values, it helps to anchor on how iterations are counted, because that is what makes the behavior predictable.

 One iteration equals one foundation model call. The loop always ends with a single answer-generation call. A value of n buys up to n minus 1 agentic planning rounds, with the last iteration reserved for generating the response. Each planning round is one query rewrite plus a retrieval. More iterations means more planning rounds and better results on hard questions. Fewer iterations means lower latency.

 One thing that doesn’t count: speculative retrieval. The initial retrieval that runs ahead of the first planning step is retrieval, not an iteration. It never counts against your maxAgentIteration value, and it only ever makes a request faster. Keep that distinction in mind as you read the following values.

 What’s new

 The range is now 0–5.

 All three modes support multiple knowledge bases, including maxAgentIteration=0 and 1 . Single-shot retrieval doesn’t mean a single knowledge base. Agentic mode adds query decomposition, evidence evaluation, and iterative searches, rather than exclusive access to multiple knowledge bases.

 maxAgentIteration = 1: Basic RAG (the headline use case)

 This is single-shot RAG: one retrieval, then one answer. No agentic planning, no query rewriting. The API retrieves once against your query and generates a response grounded in those passages. This is the retrieve once, then generate a response pattern that previously wasn’t expressible through this API.

 Pair it with generateResponse=true to get a generated answer grounded in the retrieved passages. If you only need the passages, use maxAgentIteration=0 instead, as described in the next section.

 If most of your traffic is well-scoped, direct questions, this is likely the setting you want as a default.

 maxAgentIteration = 0: Passages only, zero LLM calls

 This runs one guaranteed retrieval and generates nothing. No foundation model is invoked. It is equivalent to calling the Retrieve API directly. This makes it most useful for callers who are already standardized on AgenticRetrieveStream and would rather change a parameter than switch APIs.

 Because no large language model (LLM) is called, there is no answer to generate. Setting generateResponse=true at this value is invalid and returns a 4xx error, because generating an answer requires an LLM call.

 maxAgentIteration = 2 to 5: Agentic mode, unchanged

 In agentic mode , a foundation model breaks complex questions into focused sub-queries and retrieves evidence in multiple steps, including across multiple knowledge bases. It evaluates the retrieved information and can refine its searches when evidence is missing. This approach can improve retrieval accuracy for multi-part and comparative questions that a single search might not fully address.

 With response generation enabled, a value of n allows up to n minus 1 planning rounds before generating an answer grounded in the retrieved evidence. Existing requests using values from 2–5 retain their current behavior.

 Choosing a value

 One way to reason about it:

 maxAgentIteration 
 What you get 
 Best for 

 0 
 One retrieval, no generation, zero LLM calls 
 Passage retrieval. Callers standardized on this API who want Retrieve-style behavior 

 1 
 One retrieval plus one answer 
 Single-shot RAG for direct, well-scoped questions 

 2 to 5 
 Up to n minus 1 planning rounds, then an answer 
 Multi-part, comparative, exploratory, and cross-knowledge-base questions 

 The lower the value, the faster and more predictable the call. The higher the value, the more the planner can decompose and refine on genuinely hard questions. Start low for simple traffic, raise it when accuracy on complex queries matters more than latency.

 In practice: An internal banking policy assistant

 Consider a fictional bank whose operations team uses an internal assistant backed by a knowledge base of account-opening procedures, documentation checklists, and policy guides. Employees use the assistant to locate and understand the bank’s documented requirements. The following examples illustrate how the application can select a retrieval mode for each workflow. They don’t describe a customer deployment or measured results.

 The following diagram shows how the banking assistant selects a retrieval mode for each request.

 Figure 1: How the banking assistant selects a retrieval mode for each request

 An employee asks the assistant a question. The application chooses a retrieval mode and sends the request to AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches the knowledge base once and generates an answer. With agentic retrieval, the service splits the question into parts, searches several times, and then generates an answer with citations. With retrieval-only, the service returns source passages without generating an answer. The following sections explain each mode.

 Answer a direct documentation question

 An employee asks, “What documents are required to open a business checking account for a sole proprietor?” In this example, the bank maintains a dedicated checklist that contains the answer. The application sets maxAgentIteration=1 and generateResponse=true to retrieve relevant passages and generate a response, without query rewriting or agentic planning.

 This is the single-shot RAG pattern: one retrieval, followed by one answer-generation call. It avoids a planning step when the question and supporting content are already well scoped.

 Compare requirements across policy documents

items.title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: A seven-layer composable reference architecture for taking enterprise agentic AI from prototype to production on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each layer has a stable contract, so you can swap technologies at any layer without redesigning the rest of the stack.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review.

 That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on.

 This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale.

 Composable architecture

 The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale.

 Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework

 Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation.

 Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic.

 Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. Splitting responsibilities keeps each agent’s context focused and makes latency more predictable. You can also test each agent’s behavior, scale it, and define its security model independently. Enforce bounded autonomy: specialists should execute strictly within the tools they have been granted, and nothing more.

 In addition to decomposing into specific specialists and setting its boundary, decouple the specialist agents from the supervisor agents. Allow the supervisor to discover the specialists from a centralized agent registry and invoke them through a standardized protocol like MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent to Agent). Maintain a centralized agent registry that catalogs every agent’s tools, skills, and owner. This gives your organization the visibility it needs for governance at scale, increases the velocity of AI agent implementation through reusability, and avoids the cost of repetitive development. Consider using Strands Agents for specialists, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the orchestrator, AWS Agent Registry and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for centralized discovery and routing.

 Security and Guardrails should be a primary concern, built into the design from day one. Agentic AI exposes organizations to a new class of risks that conventional security frameworks were not built to address, from prompt injection and tool misuse to memory and data poisoning. Treat all external content as untrusted by default. Authenticate every request, whether it comes from a user, another agent, or an automated workflow, through a service like Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . Then use fine-grained access control to determine whether each tool call is permitted before execution. Grant agents temporary, scoped credentials instead of persistent secrets. On the data-protection side, mask sensitive data like PHI (Personal Health Information) and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in agent and tool requests and responses, so that sensitive customer information does not appear in agent outputs or lingers in memory. For accountability, capture every significant decision in a tamper-evident audit trail, route high-impact actions through a human approval gate, and deploy circuit breakers to halt anomalous behavior before it can escalate. Consider using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for user inputs, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for authentication and access control, along with AWS Security and governance controls to bring defense-in-depth security.

 Application is where the end-user experience lives, whether that is a chat interface, an API surface, or an embedded widget. Keep this layer intentionally thin. Its only responsibilities should be presenting the conversation and passing requests to the orchestration layer beneath it. Resist the urge to embed business logic here. The cleaner the separation, the more easily you can iterate on the user experience without destabilizing the backend. A decision model can sit at this boundary as a fast, inexpensive check: in one call it scores whether a request is in scope, needs a human, or is urgent, returning probabilities instead of free text. Your code acts on those scores with simple thresholds, answering off-topic requests directly and flagging escalations, so the full agentic loop runs only when it adds value. When building the application layer, think about what would be needed for another AI agent to consume and interact with your AI agents along with humans. Build your external interfaces accordingly.

 Observability should watch every layer from day one, not after the first incident. Along with the logs and metrics, end-to-end agent traces are critical to measure whether the agent performed its task correctly. Along with the trace, collect cost and token usage per request, time to first token, whether the call is secure, and surface dashboards for latency, error rates, and spend before you go live. Proactive monitoring is cheaper than reactive firefighting. Consider using Amazon CloudWatch with OpenTelemetry along with Amazon CloudWatch Omni for tracing and metrics to get comprehensive visibility across your stack.

 Agentic Operations closes the loop with continuous evaluation, so set it up from day one. Score every production session for groundedness, accuracy, and safety, and put a regression gate in place to catch quality drops before they reach customers. Without this, you only know the agent worked at launch. With it, you can prove it still works after every subsequent release. Consider using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations for scoring and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore optimization for continuous performance tuning.

 To bring the architecture to life, the framework includes a ready-to-run reference implementation based on a retail customer support scenario covering order status and refund eligibility. We chose this use case because it exercises every layer of the stack while remaining intuitive enough for a team to follow and adapt to their own needs.

items.title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.summary: CrossnoKaye brought physical AI to heavy industry with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Its ATLAS platform and AURA agentic system ground AI reasoning in live plant data and run verifiable Python in isolated AgentCore sandboxes, giving plant engineers checkable, math-backed answers instead of model guesses.
items.content:
Artificial Intelligence 

 How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network.

 CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary.

 Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production.

 Solution overview

 ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS.

 Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

 ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers:

 First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) . If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster.

 Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Closed-loop optimization applications run on top of the base control layer, combining those derived synthetic readings with physics models, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning, utility tariffs, and weather forecasts to compute optimal setpoint schedules. Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues order every schedule and state update by facility before dispatching setpoints to the local base control narrative on the edge cluster, which CrossnoKaye reports runs 650,000 closed-loop control actions per day.

 Third, AURA runs inside the platform boundary on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) as microservices and durable Temporal workflows. Under the caller’s enterprise permissions, AURA agents query the internal Atlas Data gateway to read the operational state of a facility or fleet in one consistent model: upstream and downstream equipment topology, the deployed base control narratives and interlocks, physical I/O and synthetic readings, setting change and alarm histories, active optimization schedules, and plant documentation indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases .

 Having the equipment layout, the base control logic, and the sensor data in the same system makes a concrete difference when diagnosing plant issues. At an aggregates quarry running primary, secondary, and tertiary rock crushers, the back half of the plant tripped twice in a single shift. From the control room, operators saw the secondary crusher fault, cleared the alarm, and restarted the line, only for it to trip again hours later. In the historian timestamps alone, the secondary crusher faulted seconds after the tertiary crusher, which made it look like a crusher problem. Because AURA also reads the conveyor layout and the deployed base control interlocks, its investigation followed the actual control logic. A recirculating belt beneath the tertiary crusher was slipping, which tripped the tertiary crusher’s overload interlock. That interlock’s upstream safety interlock immediately halted the secondary crusher to prevent burying a stopped downstream crusher in stone. Instead of chasing a phantom crusher fault, the plant manager sent an operator to inspect the recirculating belt, confirming and fixing the slip in minutes.

 The numbered flows in Figure 1 trace how an AURA investigation runs on AWS:

 Client and edge ingress: Engineers and Model Context Protocol (MCP) clients connect through AWS WAF and a public Application Load Balancer, where the API gateway validates enterprise single sign-on (SSO) or MCP credentials. Edge telemetry and control schedules flow through Amazon VPC Lattice (authenticated with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Signature Version 4 (SigV4)) and Amazon MSK.

 Context retrieval and guarded inference: AURA workflows read plant state through the Atlas Data gateway and route prompts and organization-scoped Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) queries through the Model Gateway to foundation models, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

 Runtime computation dispatch: For statistical, thermodynamic, or multi-dataset math, the workflow streams input datasets over gRPC to AURA’s internal Sandbox Orchestrator service.

 Session coordination and live streaming: In interactive sessions, the Sandbox Orchestrator tracks active sandbox session IDs and streams live progress through Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey.

 Isolated Python execution: The Sandbox Orchestrator uses the AWS SDK to call the endpoint for the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, staging datasets and running model-authored Python inside an isolated code interpreter microVM.

 Artifact storage and Brief delivery: Verified Apache Parquet outputs, charts, and cited Briefs are saved to Amazon S3 over AWS PrivateLink , and Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) delivers automated Briefs to plant teams.

 Walkthrough

 AURA combines foundation models on Amazon Bedrock (for model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide) with isolated Python sandboxes in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, across three operational modes:

 Chats: Interactive, multi-turn engineering conversations spanning a single unit, a process line, or a multi-site portfolio (up to 200 facilities in a single turn).

 Tasks: Repeatable, parameterized investigations bound to immutable version snapshots that produce structured technical Briefs with cited evidence tables and charts.
