items.title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
items.content:
01 Reasoning through geometric problems 

 A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We collaborated with Diode Computers , 1 a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish.
 Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.

 To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.
 For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use.
 Claude went through a similar process to build the voice-assistant hub and the virtual pet, and both are also still in good working order. Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications.
 The three devices built from Claude’s designs, from left to right: a battery-powered handheld pet, a home voice-assistant hub, and a USB speakerphone. Claude engineered the electronics and the enclosures and wrote firmware for each one.

 Reasoning through geometric problems
 The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.
 Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient.
 To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on BenchCAD 2.1 , a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1.
 Scores plotted against total API cost for recent frontier models on Diode PCB Gym, a benchmark that instructs models to place components and route connections on circuit boards whose layouts have been removed.

 Revising designs
 Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.
 When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers.
 And when placing tracks in its design file for the voice-assistant hub, Claude noticed that the copper connections were “getting too tangled to trace visually” and reasoned, “I should just rip these traces [tracks] and start fresh.” It proceeded to delete and reroute copper connections dozens of times until it found an arrangement that worked.
 The routing for the voice-assistant hub before and after Claude reorganized the connections. Left: the microphone’s power track (blue lines) loops around the ground ring at the sound port, a front-side track (red) crosses the ring, and a via—a small hole that connects layers of copper—is placed between the microphone’s pads. Right: the same area after Claude rerouted the power track, with the ring clear and grounded. Claude’s reasoning for redoing the version on the left: “That’s risky placement under a bottom-port MEMS mic, even if clearance is technically fine, so I want to redo the local routing cleanly for both identical mic footprints.”

 Using software and documentation
 When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place. 2 
 To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.
 Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track. Within about half an hour, Claude had a router that could lay each long track in roughly a second. When Claude spotted an audio clock track running too close to the Ethernet tracks, it adjusted the router to leave more room around sensitive tracks.
 Keeping track of constraints and downstream effects
 Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. For example, it found that the speakerphone’s board couldn’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch would hit the back wall. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.
 When designing the enclosure for the voice-assistant hub, Claude calculated that a 25 mm-long microphone port—the opening that lets sound reach the microphone—would resonate near 3.4 kHz. That is “right in the voice band,” it reasoned, “which is not ideal though still usable for voice assistant purposes. A better approach is a wedge-shaped enclosure that’s tall at the rear and steps down low at the front.” The wedge shape shortened the ports to about 10 mm, which raised the resonant frequency to about 8.9 kHz, at the very edge of the range used for speech. Claude also wrote firmware for the speakerphone that dims its ring of LED lights as the audio becomes louder, to keep the device under the electrical current limit Claude had designed into the board.
 Claude’s designs for the home voice-assistant hub and the finished prototype. Claude wrote the code that modeled the case in CAD, laid out the circuit board, and wrote the firmware.

 In electronics design, engineers have to work within the constraints of the real world. That is, they have to make sure a factory can actually make the thing they want to bu

 Multi-agent teams can solve challenging, long-horizon problems. In September , we published the first end-to-end formalization of Fermatâs Last Theorem, written by dozens of agents running an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1. That work relied on Prove2Me, a platform for formalizing mathematics, and direction from a researcher. In a new toy experiment, a team of 1,000 agents running an early version of Claude Fable 5.2 reproduced the proof without the scaffolding provided by Prove2Me or steering from a researcher. The team took 28.7 hours, used one-third as many output tokens, and wrote a proof one-seventh the length of the original.

 Each agent worked in a sandbox with no internet access. A classifier checked every shell command and file edit before it ran, and an offline monitor reviewed each of the teamâs actions. We gave the agents a list of 60 statements, a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, the definitions those statements use, and 47 proved lemmas from our earlier formalization, and assigned lead and helper roles. We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.

 This toy experiment suggests that teams of agents running models like Fable 5.2 can accomplish ambitious, long-horizon goals within carefully designed safety boundaries.

 PROBLEM

 Fermatâs Last Theorem states that no positive integers a, b, and c satisfy aâ¿ + bâ¿ = câ¿ for any n greater than 2. It remained unproven for more than 350 years, until Sir Andrew Wilesâs 129-page proof in 1995. Formalizing the proofâmaking every step checkable by a computerâhas been a long-standing goal in the mathematics community.

 Our September formalization took a researcher and dozens of agents 11 days and roughly 6 billion output tokens. They wrote 13 million lines of code in Lean, a programming language in which a computer checks every step of a proof.

 The agents coordinated through Prove2Me, a platform designed by Tianyi Peng (who is now a member of technical staff at Anthropic) and his collaborators at Columbia University. Prove2Me uses a shared graph that links each statement to be proved to the smaller statements it was split into. Any agent could split a statement, and other agents could ask the graph which unproved pieces were ready to work on, which kept them from losing track of the project state. Each statement and its proof were kept in a separate file that compiled independently, so many agents could work in parallel without editing the same files.

 HARNESS

 We wanted to see whether a team of agents running on models like Fable 5.2 could produce this result without Prove2Me or a researcher directing the work, using a harness built from general-purpose tools.

 Tools

 For this task, we gave the team of 1,000 agents 60 statements to prove, including the final theorem and 59 intermediate milestones. For each statement, the agents had to write a proof in Lean, build and check it with Leanâs tools, and submit it to the shared main branch on Git, where a grader checked it. We gave each agent the following tools:

 A shell and a file editor, in its own sandbox with no network access.

 Leanâs toolchain and Mathlib , built into the sandbox image.

 Its own Git branch, plus the ability to open merge requests into main.

 A shared Postgres database, reached from the shell.

 Collaboration

 Work on the proof can be split up, making it a good task for a multi-agent team. But agents also need to coordinate, both to build on one anotherâs work and to avoid duplicating it. In our original formalization , Claudeâs early attempts failed because agents lost track of the projectâs state and stopped collaborating effectively. Moving to the Prove2Me platform solved this problem.

 For this run, each agent had a sandbox on its own lightweight virtual machine. A single shared machine hit its limits at about 100 agents: more than half of our 100-agent runs had to be stopped or restarted because memory, disk, or CPU ran out.

 With 1,000 separate sandboxes, the agents needed a way to share their work, so we gave them a SQL database (Figure 1). We chose SQL because it offers general primitives for organizing information, its transactions handle concurrent writes from 1,000 agents, and Claude is already familiar with it. The agents used the database to claim tasks, share notes, and log finished work.

 FIG 1 Each of the 1,000 agents ran in its own sandbox, connected to the outside only by a pipe to a gateway. The gateway called the Claude API and passed Git and SQL requests to the shared repository and database. 
 Prompting

 Our prompt gave Claude a list of 60 statements to prove, each with a one-line informal description, and described the available tools (listed above).

 The only structure we gave the team was a hierarchy, consisting of one lead and 999 helpers. We told the lead to split the problem into parts and assign them to the helpers. We told the helpers to expect work from the lead and to check with the lead if a task was unclear.

 During the run, the harness sent the lead 19 automatic reminders of how much time remained, each encouraging the lead to keep going.

 SAFETY

 As weâve shared previously , no single layer of defense is sufficient to contain a team of agents. In this experiment, we combined sandboxing with real-time and offline monitoring to keep each agent in its own virtual machine with no network access and to detect any attempts to escape the sandbox or tamper with monitoring.

 Sandboxing

 We secured each agentâs sandbox in the following ways (Figure 2):

 Communication : Agents had no dedicated messaging tools and coordinated only through the database and Git.

 Code changes : An agent could push only to its own Git branch and open a merge request into main. A separate job then merged the changes into main, refusing them only in cases of a conflict or a fault, such as unrelated history.

 Database access : Database calls ran under a shared unprivileged role. Each SQL statement had a five-second time limit, and writes were refused above 256 MiB.

 Network controls : Sandboxes did not have network access. Their one link out was a pipe to the gateway, which relayed their requests.

 Identity : The gateway tagged each request with the agentâs identity outside the sandbox, to prevent one agent from posing as another.

 Kernel : Each sandboxâs kernel was built without features that give a root user a direct path into it, such as loadable modules, kexec, raw memory access, and kernel probes. It ran in kernel lockdown mode.

 Least privilege : Each agentâs commands ran inside its sandbox as an unprivileged user, with tools like sudo that could regain root removed. The agentâs tools were designed so they couldnât read or change the agent loop that ran them.

 FIG 2 Three safety layers surrounded the team: sandboxing, real-time monitoring, and offline monitoring. A classifier checked each tool call before it ran, and an offline monitor reviewed the teamâs actions. 
 Real-time monitoring

 To make runs like this safer, we use a prompted LLM classifier that can block each tool call, including shell commands and file edits. The classifier watches for attempts to escape the sandbox, probe its boundaries, or tamper with monitoring, and for any harmful actions the model might take if it manages to exit the sandbox. When the classifier blocks a tool call, the whole agent team stops and a person must review the block before the team can restart. This is intended to prevent another agent from carrying out a blocked action.

 To test whether our classifier could detect sophisticated sabotage, we ran multi-agent side-task and sabotage evaluations, in which red-team agents used strategies like decomposition attacks to try to fool the classifier into permitting a sandbox escape. We found that monitors that viewed the agentsâ chain of thought (CoT) and interagent communication were able to detect all sabotage attempts in these evaluations, so we now use them to monitor our multi-agent runs. In parallel, we run an action-based version of the same monitorâwhich sees only actions, not CoTâto guard against an agentâs reasoning persuading the monitor to permit a harmful action.

 Weâre continuing to improve our monitoring stack through human-guided and automatic red-teaming, by evaluating it against production transcripts, including past incidents, and by expanding our threat modeling. In the run in this post, we used only the action-based monitor. Only a block on the lead would have ended the run; a block on a helper removed just that helper.

 Shortly after this run, we added the parallel CoT monitor. We run experiments like this on models that may not have completed our pre-release alignment assessment, so we design our monitoring for the possibility that a model is misaligned. Models we release complete that assessment first, which reduces this risk but doesnât eliminate it.

 Across more than a million tool calls, none in this run met the bar to be blocked. When we replayed these calls against the CoT monitor and todayâs rubric, only one, a check for root access, came close to being bloc

 The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs.

 If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code, you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs.

 FIG A One photo of an alley, rendered in code by Claude Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2. Each image is a Python program the model wrote, calling a drawing engine it also wrote, shown from first layer to finished. Demo by Lance Martin. 
 TL;DR

 The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium .

 There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work.

 From there:

 Move down to Sonnet 5.5 for well-scoped everyday work, like a bug fix or a feature built against a spec. Just because you have a clear spec doesn't mean you should use Sonnet, though. A migration or a performance optimization can have clear specs and still be difficult enough to warrant Opus 5.5, or Fable 5.2 for a major one.

 Move further down to Haiku 5.5 for the simplest high-volume work, such as classification, routing, and extraction. Haiku 5.5 is also good to use with subagents that work on a larger model's side tasks.

 Move up to Claude Fable 5.2 for the hardest technical projects in coding, finance and the sciences. Also move up when Opus 5.5 at high still falls short, or for long unattended runs.

 Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate.

 Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model.

 PICK A MODEL BY TASK

 Task Starting model Starting effort Why 
 Everyday engineering and debugging. Multi-PR feature work Opus 5.5 medium (default), then high Balance of cost and capability for everyday tasks. 
 Classification, routing, tagging, and high volume extraction Haiku 5.5 medium (default) Lowest cost and latency in the model family. 
 Subagents that search files, read logs, or summarize Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 The model's default Wrong answers are cheap to spot, and the main model has the judgment calls anyway. 
 Chat and interactive sessions Sonnet 5.5 (or Haiku 5.5 for simple chat at volume) low or medium Sonnet 5.5 is fast, especially on low or medium effort. 
 Well-scoped coding, like bug fixes, feature iteration, and spec driven work Sonnet 5.5 medium , then high for harder tasks It handles scoped tasks well at half the Opus 5.5 token price. 
 Everyday documents, slides, and spreadsheets Sonnet 5.5 high (default; medium in Claude Code) It iterates fast and has a strong eye for design. For a complex financial model, or a document built from a large pile of source material, start on Opus 5.5. 
 Agent tasks you run repeatedly such as investigation, review, or drafting Sonnet 5.5 medium Well-defined, repeated tasks rarely need a bigger model. 
 Computer use and vision-heavy workflows Opus 5.5 medium These runs are long agentic loops over many screenshots and images, the kind of long-running agentic work Opus 5.5 is built for. 
 Major refactors and migrations, architecture planning, and leading many subagents Fable 5.2 medium , then high (the API default is high ) It's Anthropic's most capable generally available model for technical fields.

 You aren't sure yet Opus 5.5 medium (default) Claude Code uses it by default on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise and the Anthropic API, and the platform docs recommend it as the starting point.

 Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page .

 FIG B Claude Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 each build the same portfolio site, shown side by side. Demo by Addy Osmani. 
 THE TRADE-OFFS

 When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through.

 Capability and cost per finished task

 Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level.

 A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in Spending your effort , on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens.

 On the hardest work, the price gap can close. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high scored about level with Opus 5.5 at max (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. So before you raise Opus 5.5 past high on a hard task, test Fable 5.2. For everyday work, Opus 5.5 at medium is still the place to start. For benchmark results, see the launch post .

 However, the Claude Platform's cost and intelligence measurements also show the limits of a small model. These generally do well on high-volume work with checkable outputs and are less suited to long agentic loops.

 When you compare two models, price the hardest tasks in your set as well as the typical ones, because the hardest tasks carry most of the spend. On one 20-problem search benchmark, two problems carried 43% of the spend.

 FIG C Fable 5.2 shows how a game engine builds a world. It draws one 3D scene in sixteen looks, from wireframe and pixel art to ray tracing, and labels each technique. Demo by Dan Fein. 
 Latency against accuracy

 A faster setup finishes sooner and can miss more. Think through how long a person can wait before you pick your model and effort level. For replies a person waits on, start Sonnet 5.5 at low or medium .

 Often next generation models are faster than their predecessors. Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1. Sonnet 5.5 runs 30% faster than Sonnet 5.

 Effort level and latency are roughly correlated. Determine if the accuracy you gain is worth the extra latency. For example, on SWE-bench Pro, Opus 5.5 at medium scored about 2.5 points lower for about 70% of the cost as the high effort setting. At low it scored about 8 points lower for about a third of the cost. At xhigh it scored about 1.4 points higher for 2.5 times the cost of high .

 Often providing a means of self-verification is more cost effective and adds less latency than changing effort levels. When a model isn't good enough for a task, take these steps in order:

 Check that the model can verify its own work, with a test, a build or a script that calls the endpoint.

 Raise effort one level.

 Move to the next model up, starting at a lower effort level than you used on the smaller one.

 If you can check outcomes automatically, run everything at a low level and re-run only the failures at a high one. On the same SWE-bench Pro subset, Opus 5.5 at low with failures re-run at high passed about 97% of tasks for about $0.17 each, against 95.3% for $0.29 with every task at high .

 If you need a faster reply from the same model, you can pay for speed instead of giving up capability. On the Claude API, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 both offer fast mode , with higher output speed at premium pricing.

Exploring the world's languages with Language Explorer

 November 9, 2026
 Daan van Esch, Senior Technical Program Manager, Google DeepMind and Uche Okonkwo, Senior Program Manager, Google Research

 Language Explorer, featured in an exhibition at the Museum of Communication in Berlin, Germany, lets you explore the world's linguistic diversity online through visualizations and data.

 Our world has a fascinating wealth of languages, and for over two decades, Google has been building language technologies that cover as many languages as possible. In 2006, we started a small experiment with Google Translate, supporting just two languages (English and Arabic) at the time. Fast forward to today: nearly 250 languages are supported, with around a trillion words translated every month . Our commitment to linguistic diversity runs across products, all in service of our mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful. Building products that reflect the world's linguistic diversity takes far more than software engineering; it requires close collaboration with the communities we aim to serve, building in a way that's deeply aligned and respectful of local communities, heritage, history, values and context. This is why we've been working on grassroots initiatives like Project Vaani in India and Project Waxal in Africa, partnering with local organizations to collect thousands of hours of open speech data across underserved languages.
 But gathering this data is only one part of the journey. Preserving language vitality requires working closely with native speakers, academic institutions, and cultural organizations. Partnerships, such as our coalition with the Gates Foundation , ensure that modern digital tools reflect the nuances and authentic voices of their communities. Expanding language coverage responsibly also requires deeply understanding linguistic diversity on a global scale. This approach enables products like Gboard , our Android keyboard, to support 900+ language varieties.
 To better appreciate the breadth and complexity of this speech diversity, we've been working on a tool to help visualize the world's linguistic diversity, inspired by earlier visualization initiatives like Google Earth . The Language Explorer is an interactive web platform designed to let researchers, educators, and language enthusiasts discover and visualize linguistic diversity around the world. Developed as part of our 1,000 Languages Initiative , the Language Explorer brings together data across thousands of languages, building on our open-source LinguaMeta dataset .

 This week marks the opening of a new major exhibition at the Museum of Communication Berlin, Real Talk! Language. Power. World. ( Real Talk! Sprache. Macht. Welt. ) featuring the Language Explorer as an interactive installation. The exhibition explores how language shapes identity, society, and technology across a multi-year run in Berlin (through February 2028) and at the Museum of Communication Frankfurt (through September 2029). The Language Explorer installation reflects our broader work to build AI and language technologies that serve everyone, regardless of what language they speak, read, or sign .
 If you can't make it to the exhibition in person, you can explore the museum's themes via an online companion starting November 6th, or dive directly into the world's rich linguistic diversity online with the Language Explorer .

 Make a Robot Arm Feel Weightless with NVIDIA Holoscan 5

 Build a responsive gravity-compensation loop with Pinocchio, a Seeed Studio reBot arm, using a simple Holoscan graph in Python or C++

 Nov 09, 2026

 By Jay Carlson and Ansley Dunn 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA Holoscan 5 enables low-latency robotic control and high-throughput perception in a single programming model with execution paths for CPU and GPU workloads.
 A gravity-compensation loop built from three custom Holoscan operators reads joint state at 400 Hz, computes inverse dynamics with Pinocchio , and sends torque commands to the Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601-DM using the motorbridge library.
 Holoscan partitions group the operators on one thread to avoid cross-thread handoffs, and drop-oldest queues prevent outdated samples from accumulating.
 Nsight Systems profiling with built-in NVTX annotations shows pinning the control partition to a CPU core reduces p99.99 latency by roughly 5x for C++ and 9.6x for Python implementations.
 Next Steps
 Download the Holoscan 5 SDK to begin developing robotic control applications.
 Follow the gravity compensation tutorial to build and run the complete example on supported hardware.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 Picture guiding a robot arm by hand while its motors supply just enough torque to support its weight and keep the robot upright. This simple interaction, a useful starting point for robots that learn by demonstration, manipulate objects, or work alongside people, depends on a gravity-compensation loop. 

 Building such a loop is only possible by continuously calculating the inverse dynamics of the system based on precise models of all the links of the robot arm, their dimensions, masses, and moments of inertia. This calculation, which needs to be done rapidly with low jitter, requires knowing the current state of the robot, so gravity-comp demos are an excellent proof of life for both the robot model and the runtime that’s executing these algorithms.

 NVIDIA Holoscan 5 introduced robotic control alongside streamlined sensor processing. In this tutorial, we’ll build custom Holoscan SDK operators and wire them into a graph. We’ll test the code on a real robot and use the Holoscan SDK’s built-in Nsight Systems annotations to inspect latency and jitter.

 This walkthrough has been tested on Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson Thor, and x86 Ubuntu 24.04 systems.

 Why Holoscan? 

 Video 1. A responsive robot with Holoscan installed for gravity compensation workload vs. a custom script runtime 

 Holoscan SDK brings low-latency control and high-throughput perception into one programming model , with execution paths designed for CPU- and GPU-based workloads. Its goal is a transparent runtime: minimize avoidable framework overhead while making application execution explicit and inspectable.

 Keep the control path focused on the work. Holoscan uses partitions to group chains of operators on a single thread, avoiding cross-thread handoffs and unnecessary syscalls, reducing latency and jitter. Clock and data-arrival triggers express when work should run, while bounded, drop-oldest queues prevent outdated work from accumulating.

 Bring existing algorithms and code rather than rewriting them for a framework. Holoscan 5 has a new, lightweight programming model that can be easily integrated into existing code bases, and it’s never been easier to get data into and out of Holoscan graphs.

 Add perception without adopting a different programming model. Whether you’re handling 10 kHz CPU-centric motor control loops, heavy-throughput GPU algorithms, or AI inference, Holoscan lets developers and their agents clearly express execution intent using the same operators, ports, and graph APIs, logically splitting their workloads into separate graphs that can coexist, with the ability to pin partitions to dedicated CPU cores, CUDA green contexts, or even execute as a CUDA graph.

 Inspect the plan, then measure the result. Operators express their intent with timing contracts, and before the first run, the compiled plan exposes how the application will execute and catches configuration errors before deployment. This means agents and developers can quickly iterate on a design without ever deploying to real hardware. Plus, built-in NVTX annotations make operator execution and message transfers visible in Nsight Systems. Developers can examine host control-path latency and update jitter, then repeat those measurements as the application grows.

 An accessible platform for torque-control development 

 This tutorial is built around the Seeed Studio reBot Arm B601-DM , which is an accessible, affordable platform for getting started with modern robotics control. Most low-cost robot arm development platforms use highly-geared hobby servos, which are only suitable for positional control. The reBot Arm uses quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators that provide high torque bandwidth for both control and sensing — important for haptic, co-bot, or other torque-oriented projects like this one.

 Starting off with gravity-comp 

 Before adding perception pipelines, motion planners, and other higher-level controls, building a basic gravity compensation loop helps provide a useful (and entertaining!) sanity-check for whether your simulation model accurately describes the physical robot. While position-control examples can mask problems with joint axes, offsets, link placements, masses, and moments, all of these affect the required torque in instantly-observable ways; any bugs in DH parameters or mass properties can make the arm sag or push upward as its pose changes.

 Even if your end application doesn’t need gravity-comp, torque control lets us shape how the robot responds to forces—a key ingredient in safer interaction between humans and co-bots. Our arm combines gravity feedforward with light stiffness and damping, so it supports its weight while yielding to a person’s hand.

 That flexibility makes timing critical. Tracking a position through torque commands requires rapid, consistent feedback at hundreds or thousands of Hz, and runtime overhead and thread handoffs can add phase lag and jitter that cause the robot to become unstable.

 This tutorial uses Pinocchio as the inverse-dynamics solver. It loads the robot’s URDF model and provides a Recursive Newton–Euler Algorithm (RNEA) solver, which calculates joint torques for specified positions, velocities, and accelerations. We also use the motorbridge library to read joint feedback and send commands to the arm’s motors.

 Set up the Python example 

 This walkthrough uses Holoscan’s Python API. The tutorial repository also contains a complete C++ implementation , with its own build instructions . Both implement the same three-operator control loop.

 Use Python 3.12 or newer on Linux. From the repository root:

 python3.12 -m venv build/python-venv
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip install --only-binary=:all: -r requirements-python.txt
build/python-venv/bin/python -m pip check 

 Check the serial device and motor IDs in the arm’s configuration file. The tutorial repository’s technical guide covers configuration, the math, and hardware startup.

 Express the control loop as three operators 

 Holoscan 5 has two programming concepts: Operators and Graphs. To read the robot’s state, calculate the command using the inverse-dynamics solver, and send it to the arm, we can decompose that problem into three operators wired into a graph:

 Figure 1. Closed loop control system diagram 

 Operators are subclassed from Operator and have three important methods to implement:

 Method Purpose 
 setup() Declare input and output ports. 
 contract() Declare when to run and which input data to use. 
 compute() Read input(s), do work, and publish output(s). 

 Table 1. Core methods to implement for custom Holoscan operators 

 Here are outlines of the three operators to build:

 1. Read joint state on a clock 

 JointStateSourceOp declares one output in setup() . Its OnClock contract requests a tick every 2.5 ms (we’re running this demo at 400 Hz). Each compute() reads all seven motors and emits their state:

 import holoscan as hsdk

class JointStateSourceOp(hsdk.Operator):
 state = hsdk.Output("state", hsdk.pyobject)

 def setup(self, spec):
 spec.output(self.state)

 def contract(self):
 return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnClock(period=hsdk.time.us(2500)))

 def start(self):
 self.sequence = 0

 def compute(self, ctx):
 self.sequence += 1
 self.state.emit(robot.read_state(self.sequence)) 

 2. Compute gravity compensation when state arrives 

 PinocchioGravityOp declares a state input and command output. OnEach runs it when state arrives. The hsdk.Param declarations expose gains, torque scaling, and joint direction as operator parameters:

 class PinocchioGravityOp(hsdk.Operator):
 state = hsdk.Input("state", hsdk.pyobject)
 command = hsdk.Output("command", hsdk.pyobject)
 kp = hsdk.Param(1.5, range=(0.0, 500.0))
 kd = hsdk.Param(1.0, range=(0.0, 5.0))
 tau_scale = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6)
 joint_direction = hsdk.Param([1.0] * 6)

 def setup(self, spec):
 spec.input(self.state, queue_depth=1)
 spec.output(self.command)

 def contract(self):
 return hsdk.Contract().trigger(hsdk.OnEach(self.state))

 def compute(self, ctx):
 state = self.state.receive_data()
 command = controller.compute(
 state, kp=self.kp, kd=self.kd,
 tau_scale=self.tau_scale, joint_direction=self.joint_direction)
 self.command.emit(command)
